title: The European Fabless Semiconductor Association was formally launched today in Brussels; Semiconductor veteran Paul de Bot named its first President
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

The European Fabless Semiconductor Association launched in Brussels on November 4, giving Europe’s chip designers a dedicated voice as they seek investment, customers and greater influence over semiconductor policy.

Founded by Axelera AI, Quside, Semidynamics, SiPearl and VSORA, the association will represent companies that design chips while outsourcing manufacturing to foundries. Former TSMC executive Paul de Bot has been appointed its first president during the incubation phase. SiPearl founder and CEO Philippe Notton will chair the board.

The announcement took place at an ALLPROs event attended by European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen. The founding members have completed notary registration of the association’s articles.

According to the announcement, fabless companies account for more than 60% of the semiconductor market excluding memory, while Europe holds less than 1% of the global fabless market. The founders argue that Europe needs stronger design businesses to compete in growing markets, particularly AI and data centre computing.

The association will focus on four areas: policy representation, shared market and funding intelligence, access to investors and customers, and pooled services such as electronic design automation software licensing. It aims to attract more than 50 members within three years.

Its formation is supported by the Horizon Europe VOICES project, coordinated by Quside. The organisation is being established as an international nonprofit association under Belgian law.

The initiative matters because chip design companies need a route from research to commercial sales. Manufacturing capacity alone cannot create demand for European processors.

Founders highlighted procurement as an opportunity. European investments in AI factories, sovereign cloud infrastructure and public data centres could provide customers for competitive European chips.

The association’s impact will depend on whether collective representation produces tangible results: more growth capital, easier access to engineering tools and manufacturing partners, and purchase orders that help European designers build sustainable businesses.
